coverage: Full dedication, preface and both parts in original-en and modern-en: named historical, philosophical, literary and religious references and identified implicit references. Generic hypothetical people, political bodies and population labels are not given invented personal identities.

entities.name: Isaac Rousseau
entities.body: Rousseau’s father, the Geneva craftsman whose example he recalls in the dedication.

entities.name: Tacitus
entities.body: The Roman historian among the authors read by Rousseau’s father.

entities.name: Plutarch
entities.body: The Greek biographer whose works Rousseau recalls beside his father’s tools.

entities.name: Hugo Grotius
entities.body: The Dutch jurist and political thinker cited on law and property.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: The Greek philosopher used as a model for inquiry into humanity and nature.

entities.name: Pliny the Elder
entities.body: The Roman natural historian invoked as a model for scientific inquiry.

entities.name: Pliny the Younger
entities.body: The Roman writer quoted addressing the emperor Trajan.

entities.name: Jean-Jacques Burlamaqui
entities.body: The Genevan jurist cited on the meaning of natural right.

entities.name: Persius
entities.body: The Roman satirist quoted in the Latin verses introducing the inquiry.

entities.name: Moses
entities.body: The biblical lawgiver whose writings Rousseau invokes in discussing the state of nature.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Greek philosopher invoked as an imagined judge of the discourse and cited on medicine and government.

entities.name: Xenocrates
entities.body: The Greek philosopher and head of the Academy, imagined alongside Plato as a judge of the discourse.

entities.name: Thomas Hobbes
entities.body: The English political philosopher whose account of humanity in the state of nature Rousseau challenges.

entities.name: Montesquieu
entities.body: The French political thinker referred to as the other illustrious philosopher in the discussion of natural fear.

entities.name: Richard Cumberland
entities.body: The English philosopher and bishop cited on natural law and human behavior.

entities.name: Samuel Pufendorf
entities.body: The German natural-law thinker whose views on fear, liberty and slavery Rousseau examines.

entities.name: Francis Correal
entities.body: The travel-account author cited on the Caribs of Venezuela.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: The ancient Greek physician associated here with dietary treatment.

entities.name: Celsus
entities.body: The Roman medical writer cited on the history of diet as a treatment.

entities.name: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac
entities.body: The French philosopher whose account of language Rousseau discusses.

entities.name: Bernard Mandeville
entities.body: The author of The Fable of the Bees, cited in the argument about compassion.

entities.name: Sulla
entities.body: The Roman general and dictator used in an example of compassion coexisting with cruelty.

entities.name: Alexander of Pherae
entities.body: The Thessalian tyrant whose response to tragedy is contrasted with his cruelty.

entities.name: Juvenal
entities.body: The Roman satirist quoted in the discussion of compassion.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher invoked in the discussion of virtue and reason.

entities.name: John Locke
entities.body: The English philosopher cited on property and political authority.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: The traditional lawgiver of Sparta, used as an example of founding political institutions.

entities.name: Trajan
entities.body: The Roman emperor addressed in the quotation from Pliny the Younger.

entities.name: Brasidas
entities.body: The Spartan commander to whom Rousseau attributes the reply about the pleasures of liberty.

entities.name: Algernon Sidney
entities.body: The English republican thinker cited against deriving absolute government from fatherhood.

entities.name: Louis XIV
entities.body: The French king whose 1667 edict is quoted in the argument about rulers and law.

entities.name: Jean Barbeyrac
entities.body: The jurist cited against surrendering liberty to arbitrary power.

entities.name: Lucan
entities.body: The Roman poet quoted to illustrate obedience to a ruler’s criminal commands.

entities.name: Diogenes
entities.body: The Cynic philosopher invoked through his search for an honest human being.

entities.name: Cato the Younger
entities.body: The Roman republican statesman used as an example of virtue at odds with its age.

entities.name: The Tarquins
entities.body: The royal family associated with the last kings of Rome, whose expulsion Rousseau discusses.

entities.name: Glaucus
entities.body: The sea god whose weathered statue illustrates the difficulty of recognizing humanity’s original nature.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine creator invoked in the discussion of human nature, liberty and religious authority.

entities.name: Adam
entities.body: The first man in the biblical creation story, invoked in the discussion of the state of nature.

entities.name: Podalirius
entities.body: The Greek healer at Troy, paired with Machaon in the example about ancient medicine.

entities.name: Machaon
entities.body: The Greek healer at Troy mentioned alongside Podalirius.

entities.name: Andromache
entities.body: Hector’s wife in Trojan legend, invoked as a figure of tragic suffering.

entities.name: Priam
entities.body: The king of Troy, invoked alongside Andromache as a figure of tragic suffering.

entities.name: Ceres
entities.body: The Roman goddess of agriculture, cited through her association with law and land distribution.

entities.name: The Persian satrap
entities.body: The Persian official in the anecdote Rousseau tells about Brasidas and liberty.
